summary.title: Learning design rules for selective oxidation catalysts from highthroughput experimentation and artificial intelligence
summary.authors: Lucas Foppa; Christopher Sutton; Luca M Ghiringhelli; Sandip De; Patricia Löser; Stephan A Schunk; Ansgar Schäfer; Matthias Scheffler
summary.executive_summary: This study addresses the challenge of designing heterogeneous catalysts for the selective oxidation of propylene, a process complicated by vast materials spaces and complex reaction networks. The authors employ a high-throughput experimentation (HTE) approach to synthesize and test 120 three-component catalysts based on ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus supported on SiO2. These experimental results are combined with theoretical descriptors derived from Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations of free-atom properties. The core methodology utilizes Subgroup Discovery (SGD), an artificial intelligence technique designed to identify local patterns of exceptional performance rather than global averages. By maximizing a quality function based on the Janson-Shannon divergence, the SGD algorithm extracts specific constraints on physicochemical parameters that correlate with high yields of value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid). The analysis identifies temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity as the critical parameters governing this high performance. These derived 'SG rules' successfully guide the design of more complex four- and five-component catalysts, predicting materials with oxygenate yields up to 60%, which is significantly higher than the maximum yield observed in the training dataset. The study demonstrates that this data-driven approach can uncover interpretable, chemically meaningful rules that rationalize local reactivity patterns and accelerate the discovery of superior catalysts without requiring explicit atomistic modeling of the full catalytic progression.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study addresses the challenge of designing heterogeneous catalysts for the selective oxidation of propylene, a process complicated by vast materials spaces and complex reaction networks. The authors employ a high-throughput experimentation (HTE) approach to synthesize and test 120 three-component catalysts based on ruthenium, tungsten, and phosphorus supported on SiO2. These experimental results are combined with theoretical descriptors derived from Density Functional Theory (DFT) calculations of free-atom properties. The core methodology utilizes Subgroup Discovery (SGD), an artificial intelligence technique designed to identify local patterns of exceptional performance rather than global averages. By maximizing a quality function based on the Janson-Shannon divergence, the SGD algorithm extracts specific constraints on physicochemical parameters that correlate with high yields of value-added oxygenates (acrolein and acrylic acid). The analysis identifies temperature, phosphorus content, and composition-weighted electronegativity as the critical parameters governing this high performance. These derived 'SG rules' successfully guide the design of more complex four- and five-component catalysts, predicting materials with oxygenate yields up to 60%, which is significantly higher than the maximum yield observed in the training dataset. The study demonstrates that this data-driven approach can uncover interpretable, chemically meaningful rules that rationalize local reactivity patterns and accelerate the discovery of superior catalysts without requiring explicit atomistic modeling of the full catalytic progression.

Research Context
Heterogeneous catalysis involves complex interplays of surface reactions and dynamic restructuring. First-principles atomistic modeling of full catalytic progression is often impractical. High-throughput experimentation tests many materials but lacks guidance for the next step. The number of good catalysts is very small compared to the number of possible materials. Global models minimize average error but fail to focus on the most interesting high-performance materials. Distinct mechanisms operate depending on materials, leading to unbalanced performance distributions.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can subgroup discovery identify constraints on physicochemical parameters associated with outstanding performance? Do specific rules describe materials and conditions with high yields of oxygenates? Can these rules guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements? Will the SG rules reflect underlying processes associated with high performance? Can the approach identify promising candidates not yet synthesized by experiment?

Methodological Details
The study synthesized 120 SiO2-supported catalysts containing ruthenium, tungsten and phosphorus. Catalysts were tested in the catalytic oxidation of propylene. Candidate parameters included temperature and ten parameters related to composition and chemical nature. Descriptive parameters were derived from calculated free-atom properties using DFT. Reactions were carried out in tubular, fixed-bed reactors. The reaction feed included Ar, H2O, N2, O2 and propylene with specific molar rates. The same mass of catalyst was used in all reactions to keep contact time fixed. Catalysts were prepared on a SiO2 pseudo-liquid support. The atomic structures of all tested catalysts are not known in detail. The target variable for the analysis was the yield of oxygenates.

Procedures And Architectures
The study applies the subgroup-discovery artificialintelligence local approach. Propositions are inequalities constraining the values of continuous candidate descriptive parameters. Selectors are statements formed by a number of propositions and the AND connector. The approach maximizes a quality function that measures how outstanding specific subselections are. Free-atom properties were calculated using DFT-PBEsol and the FHI-aims code. System-specific properties are obtained by taking the composition-weighted average of per-element properties. The quality function includes a coverage term to control subgroup size. The second term is the cumulative Janson-Shannon divergence between distributions. This divergence measures dissimilarity between the subgroup and whole data set distributions. The approach focuses on exceptional high-performing materials when most data are low-performing.

Key Results
50% of measured materials result in less than 2% oxygenates yield. Only 41 measurements out of 1220 are associated to yields of oxygenates above 20%. The average oxygenates yield over the whole data set is equal to 4.83%. The maximum oxygenates yield value is 26.85%. The selected SG contains 15 data points with an average yield of 24.15%. The average yield in the SG is five times higher than the average on the whole data set. The SG is described by rules: 280 ≤ I ≤ 300℃, J K > 0.55, and 3.910 ≤ VY < 4.002 eV. The rule on temperature highlights that highest yields are observed for intermediate temperatures. The rule on phosphorus content shows that a relatively high phosphorus content is needed. The rule on electronegativity effectively limits the range of Ru contents. Four-component materials with Nb, Cr, Mo, Sn, Pb, and Sb achieve high yields at lower S2. The highest yield achieved for a four-component material is 60.19% at 400ºC. Five-component catalysts achieve yields up to twice as large as three-component materials. The highest yield for a five-component catalyst is 59.60% at 400ºC. The five-component catalyst has a composition-averaged electronegativity of 3.947 eV. SG rules for four-and five-component materials require temperatures ≥ 360 ℃. Different composition-dependent parameters are required for four-and five-component materials.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The SG rules reflect specific underlying processes resulting in outstanding performance. High phosphorus content relates to the dilution of metal active sites on a phosphate matrix. Too much Ru leads to undesired combustion products. The approach identifies generalizable rules describing exceptional performance. The identified catalysts are significantly more complex than those of the training data set. The SG rules hinted at materials that are significantly more performant than any training observation. The approach is suitable for the search of exceptional materials hardly modelled explicitly by theory.

Contradictions And Limitations
The SG rule on reaction temperature is not transferable to four-component materials. It is unclear if rules apply to arbitrary ruthenium contents. It is unclear if rules apply to elements with significantly different radii compared to tungsten. Different mechanisms may operate on these materials which could also lead to exceptional performance. The SGD analysis might need to be performed including new data points covering unexplored portions of the materials space. The oxygen content is not included in the material's characterization. The atomic structures of all tested catalysts are not known in detail.

Claims
SGD identifies interpretable, chemically meaningful rules for high-performance catalysts. The SG rules not only reflect the underlying processes particularly associated to high performance The SG rules correctly describe the experimental trend. The SG rule on the reaction temperature derived based on the three-component materials data set is thus not transferable to the four-component ones The SG rules hinted at materials that are significantly more performant that any of the observations used in training.
Complex four- and five-component catalysts can be designed using rules derived from simpler three-component data. The agreement between the SG rule and the measured oxygenate yield is reasonable in spite of the much higher materials complexity The four-and five-component outstanding catalysts achieve oxygenate yields up to twice as large as those obtained with three-component materials It is unclear if the SG rules presented in Fig. 5C can identify exceptional materials and conditions for any arbitrary ruthenium content The SG rules guide the design of more complex catalysts containing up to five elements in their composition.

Data And Code Availability
Further calculation details and values for the elemental properties used in the work available in the electronic supporting information, ESI.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
Similar SG rules are obtained when the training is performed with randomly-selected 90% of the data points. Similar SG rules are obtained when the data points presenting yield of oxygenates lower than 3% are excluded from training. The SG rules are not strongly affected by variations on the data used for their derivation.

Key Figures Tables
Fig. 1A shows the selection of subgroups of materials and conditions with the most outstanding distributions of target values. Fig. 2A and B show the propylene conversion vs. oxygenates selectivity profiles and the distribution of yield of oxygenates. Fig. 2C shows the rule on the temperature highlighting that the highest yields of oxygenates are observed for intermediate temperatures. Fig. 3B shows the ternary diagram of Ru contents limited by the rule on the composition-averaged electronegativity. Fig. 4A shows the catalyst map suggesting the use of 5.0 to 17.5 % (molar) of niobium, chromium, molybdenum, tin, lead and antimony. Fig. 5A and B show the SG presenting the highest m /no for four-and five-component HTE data.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the application of SGD to HTE and theory data to identify SG rules for high-performance catalysts. 2. The strongest evidence is the identification of a five-component catalyst with 59.60% yield, twice the training maximum. 3. The future path involves expanding the materials space to cover unexplored portions for broader rule applicability.
